Series::asin¶

Back to Series API Reference

Signature¶

Series::asin() const -> Series

What It Does¶

Applies the inverse sine elementwise.

Each input value is interpreted as a sine value and mapped back to its principal angle in radians. The principal range is [-pi / 2, pi / 2], so valid real outputs stay inside that interval.

asin() is often used after a normalization or ratio step where the result is already known to live in [-1, 1]. When that assumption is wrong, the output shows it immediately because out-of-domain values become nan.

Parameters¶

None.

This is a zero-argument transform on self.

Returns¶

Series A new Series with the same shape as self, where each element has been replaced by its principal inverse sine in radians.

Gradient¶

Mathematically, asin(x) has derivative 1 / sqrt(1 - x^2) for interior points |x| < 1.

That means:

  • the derivative is always non-negative on the real interior

  • it grows larger as the input approaches -1 or 1

On the current verified public surface used here, the reverse-mode example returns zero sensitivities. So the forward values are correct, but you should not yet rely on this method path for backward propagation.

Examples¶

Example 1. Familiar domain anchors map back to familiar angles.

std::cout << pluss::series::print(
    pluss::make_series({-1.0, -0.5, 0.0, 0.5, 1.0}).asin());

Output¶

Series(shape=[5], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=5, contiguous=true)
data=[-1.5708, -0.5236, 0.0000, 0.5236, 1.5708]

Example 2. Shape is preserved for higher-rank inputs too.

pluss::series::print(
    std::cout,
    pluss::make_series({
        {-1.0, 0.0},
        {0.5, 1.0},
    }).asin());

Output¶

Series(shape=[2,2], strides=[2,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=
⎡ -1.5708 0.0000 ⎤
⎣  0.5236 1.5708 ⎦

Example 3. The current reverse-mode path yields zero sensitivities on this surface, which should be treated as an implementation caveat rather than a mathematical property.

auto x = pluss::make_series({-0.5, 0.0, 0.5});
x.tracks_slope_(true);

auto out = x.asin();
out.sum().reverse();

std::cout << "out=" << out << "\n";
std::cout << "dx=" << x.sensitivity();

Output¶

out=pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[-0.52359878, 0, 0.52359878]
dx=pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[0, 0, 0]

Example 4. Domain violations are visible in the result.

std::cout << pluss::make_series({-1.25, -1.0, 0.0, 1.0, 1.25}).asin();

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[5], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=5, contiguous=true)
data=[nan, -1.5707963, 0, 1.5707963, nan]

Gotchas And Failure Modes¶

  • asin() is only real-valued on [-1, 1].

  • Endpoints are valid outputs, but they are numerically sharp points for the mathematical derivative.

  • The current verified backward path returns zero sensitivities here.

Summary¶

Use asin() when the data already represents sine-like values in [-1, 1] and you need principal angles back. The two practical checks are domain safety and whether your workflow needs verified gradient propagation.

See Also¶

  • Series::acos: inverse cosine on the same value domain.

  • Series::atan: inverse tangent with unrestricted real input.

  • Series::sin: forward sine transform.
